abstract: Background Gastric Cancer remains one of the most prevalent cancers worldwide, with its prognosis heavily reliant on early detection. Traditional GC diagnostic methods are invasive and risky, prompting interest in non-invasive alternatives that could enhance outcomes. Method In this study, we introduce a non-invasive approach, World Hyper-heuristic Fuzzy Deep Learning, for gastric cancer prediction using metabolomics. Metabolomics profiles of plasma samples from 702 individuals were obtained and used for classification. To apply an efficient feature selection, we employed the World Hyper Heuristic, a metaheuristic to extract the most relevant features from the dataset. Subsequently, the extracted data were classified by implementing a Fuzzy Deep Neural Network. Results The performance of WHFDL was assessed and compared against a comprehensive set of classical and state-of-the-art feature selection and classification algorithms. Our results highlighted six key metabolites as biomarkers associated with gastric cancer: (1-Methyladenosine, C18-Carnitine, Guanidineacetic acid, Hypoxanthine, Nicotinamide mononucleotide, and Succinate). The WHFDL outperformed all other classifiers, achieving an F1-score, recall and precision of 94%, 93% and 94%, respectively, along with an accuracy of 94% and an Area Under the Curve of 0.9384. Interpretability were analyzed using SHAP, LIME, IG calibration analysis, and adversarial testing, demonstrating the model’s transparency. The source code is available on ( https://github.com/arman-daliri/WHFDL ).

Overview of method, patients and dataset
The dataset [
21
] utilized in this study consists of plasma-targeted metabolomics profiles, collected from 702 individuals across three independent cohorts, including 389 gastric cancer (GC) patients and 313 non-gastric cancer (NGC) controls. Plasma samples were obtained from two Major cancer hospitals in China and were collected before any anti-cancer treatment. Cohort 1 consisted of 145 GC patients (71% Male, median age of 60 years, Stage I/II/III/IV: 52/30/53/10) and 281 NGC individuals (52% Male, median age of 50 years). Cohort 2 (
n
= 95) included 63 GC patients (76% Male, median age of 64 years, Stage I/II/III/IV: 16/14/24/9) and 32 NGC controls (88% Male, median age of 51 years). Cohort 3 only consisted of GC patients (63% Male, median age of 60 years; Stage I/II/III/IV: 40/44/89/8) and follow-up data intended for prognosis analysis were available in addition to its plasma targeted metabolomics data. This prognosis data was reported as a median follow-up period of 40 months, lacking detailed longitudinal recorded required for time-series prediction. Therefore, we excluded the follow-up data and instead utilized the metabolomics data from all three cohorts as input to our WHFDL model for GC prediction.
Plasma samples from all three cohorts underwent a standardized targeted metabolomics workflow based on liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC–MS). Following overnight fasting, blood was collected by peripheral venous sampling for Cohorts 1 and 2, and from the superior vena cava for Cohort 3. The separation of metabolites was done using a reverse-phase UPLC column, which organizes compounds based on their chemical properties. To facilitate detection of specific metabolites, the separated metabolites were then quantified using a high-sensitivity triple quadrupole mass spectrometer (AB QTRAP 6500 +) operated in multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) mode. The samples were also processed in a randomized and blinded manner during data acquisition.
To ensure analytical consistency, a quality control (QC) protocol was implemented, which involved inserting a pooled plasma sample after every ten patient samples during the LC–MS run. Metabolite signals in samples were then normalized using the ratio of global to local QC peak areas, producing relative abundance values. As a result, metabolite quantities are expressed in relation to one another rather than as absolute concentrations. Following this protocol, a total of 147 metabolites, including amino acids, organic acids, acylcarnitines, amines, nucleosides, vitamins, nucleotides and carbohydrates, were detected across all 702 plasma samples. Importantly, since the dataset was normalized and processed according to a specific QC-guided pipeline, any future application of our model requires new data to be generated and preprocessed using the same procedures described in the original study.
Using the plasma-targeted metabolomics dataset described above, we subsequently performed data analysis and applied a World Hyper-Heuristic strategy for feature selection to identify the most informative and relevant subset of features. This reinforcement learning–based method not only optimized feature selection but also contributed to handling batch effects present in the dataset. The data classification was then done using a Hierarchical Fused Fuzzy Deep Neural Network, which integrates the strengths of deep learning and fuzzy logic to effectively overcome the noise and uncertainty problems in metabolomics data.

Feature selection experimental evaluation
Given the high dimensionality of our metabolomics dataset, feature selection is an undeniably important step, as it directly impacts the model’s accuracy and predictive power by determining the quality of features provided for training. In this study, we aimed to identify the most relevant, efficient, and informative features to minimize overfitting, enhance model interpretability and computational efficiency. We reviewed four major categories of feature selection methods, including Filter methods, Wrapper methods, Embedded methods and Hybrid models

World Hyper Heuristic (WHH) falls under the Hybrid category, which combines multiple metaheuristics and uses a fitness function based on classifier accuracy to guide the feature selection process and adapt to the complexity of metabolomics data. By including both classical and more recent state-of-the-art methods, we ensured a broad and meaningful comparison across feature selection strategies.

Performance of traditional and statistical methods with feature selection
This section evaluates the performance of traditional and statistical classifiers when combined with different feature selection methods. We implemented eight widely used classification algorithms ranging from foundational to more modern ensemble and boosting-based techniques as mentioned in Table
1
. Each model was trained on feature subsets produced by five distinct feature selection techniques, in order to evaluate their impact on classification accuracy and the effectiveness of each feature selection algorithm. The resulting accuracy scores for each combination are illustrated in Fig.
5

Fig. 5
Accuracy of traditional and statistical classifiers with different feature selection methods
Among the five feature selection methods evaluated, our proposed World Hyper-Heuristic (WHH) approach demonstrated the most consistent and superior performance, achieving the highest accuracy in four out of eight classifiers: Categorical Boosting (90%), Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (90%), Decision Trees (85%) and Support Vector Classification (84%). In contrast, other methods demonstrated more limited strengths. SVM-RFE excelled in eXtreme Gradient Boosting (91%) and tied with WHH in Categorical Boosting (90%), while Boruta tied with WHH in two classifiers. Adaptive Lasso performed best in Naive Bayes (90%), and the conventional ReliefF method led only in Random Forest (90%), underperforming elsewhere due to its limitations with high-dimensional, non-linear metabolomics data. The superior performance of WHH can be attributed to its integration of metaheuristic optimization with classifier-informed feedback. Specifically, its reliance on a Support Vector Classification (SVC) accuracy-based fitness function makes it highly effective for margin-based classifiers and its ability to generate well-separated feature subsets benefits tree-based models like Decision Trees.

Each network was trained on feature subsets generated by the same five feature selection methods discussed previously, to assess how well each feature selection strategy prepares high-dimensional metabolomics data for deep architectures. The resulting classification accuracies are demonstrated in Fig.

The World Hyper-Heuristic (WHH) method demonstrated superior performance across all six deep learning architectures evaluated, achieving the highest accuracy in every case. WHH's peak performance was a 94% accuracy on the proposed WHFDL model, a seven-percentage point lead over the nearest competitor. It also led on Autoencoder Multilayer Perceptron (89%), MLP (90%), LSTM (90%), RNN (91%), and CNN (85%). The most significant performance gap was observed with CNN, a model sensitive to noisy input, where WHH's 85% accuracy notably outperformed Adaptive Lasso (76%), ReliefF (75%), and SVM-RFE (73%). This consistent superiority is attributed to WHH's capacity to integrate feature selection with representation learning by iteratively refining feature subsets using classifier feedback, framed as a reinforcement learning task. This approach provides a cleaner, more compatible input space that allows deep neural networks to focus on learning complex relationships, unlike older, traditional methods which generally performed the weakest when paired with deep architectures.

This section first examines the performance of the proposed model in comparison with other models. Then, the interpretability of the proposed model and its explanations are discussed. The proposed method is assessed in Subsection “
Classification performance experiments
” with 13 classification methods and their performance is thoroughly analyzed. In Subsection “

Classification performance experiments
To comprehensively asses classification performance, we further conducted experiments using fourteen algorithms spanning both traditional and deep learning paradigms. These included Support Vector Classification (SVC), Random Forest (RF), Decision Tree (DT), Logistic Regression (LR), Naive Bayes (NB), Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA), eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGB) and Categorical Boosting (CatB), along with deep neural networks such as our proposed World Hyper Fuzzy Deep Learning (WHFDL), Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Recurrent Neural Network (RNN, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) and Autoencoder–Multilayer Perceptron (AMLP). To ensure a fair comparison between all classification models, each model was trained on the optimal feature subset selected by WHH.
In the following, a comparative evaluation of all classifiers using precision, recall, and F1-score as the primary metrics is introduced. For each of these measures, both macro and weighted averages are also reported to ensure a more balanced and detailed analysis of model performance. Additionally, Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) plots and their corresponding Area Under the Curve (AUC) values are provided for each classification model.

It achieved the highest precision (95% for non-GC and 93% for GC), recall (96% non-GC and 90% GC), and F1-scores (96% non-GC and 92% GC), resulting in Macro and weighted averages around 94%. Traditional classifiers such as LR and SVC showed notable Limitations, particularly in detecting GC cases; LR failed to identify any GC cases, resulting in 0% precision and recall for class 1, while SVC achieved only 58% precision and similarly low recall for GC. Decision Trees and ensemble models Like RF, XGB, and CatB performed more consistently but still exhibited 10–13 percentage point drops in performance for GC detection compared to non-GC. Among deep learning models, RNN, LSTM, and MLP demonstrated relatively balanced and competitive results, achieving Macro and weighted averages between 85 and 87%, but none Matched the overall precision and recall consistency of WHFDL. CNN, on the other hand, showed a significant imbalance, particularly with recall dropping sharply from 91% for non-GC to 48% for GC detection. These findings demonstrate WHFDL’s superior ability to minimize false positives and false negatives, ensuring robust and reliable detection of both non-GC and GC cases, which is an essential requirement in clinical settings.

To further evaluate diagnostic performance, all fourteen classifiers were assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, area under the curve (AUC) scores, and confusion matrices. The ROC curves and confusion matrices for the top three performing models, WHFDL, CatB, and RNN, are shown in Fig.
7
, with full results for all models available Figure 14 in Appendix
3
. The proposed WHFDL model achieved the highest AUC score of 0.9384, indicating superior discriminative capability. CatB and RNN followed with AUCs of 0.9200 and 0.9181, respectively, while LSTM (0.9181) and MLP (0.9133) also demonstrated competitive results. Traditional classifiers such as Logistic Regression (0.79) and Decision Tree (0.75) performed weaker, reflecting limited capacity to model the non-linear and high-dimensional patterns inherent in metabolomics data. Among ensemble strategies, gradient-boosted trees such as XGB (0.89) clearly outperformed Decision Trees (0.75), highlighting the sensitivity of predictive accuracy to algorithmic refinement.
Fig. 7
Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and confusion matrices of the three best-performing classifiers
Slight inconsistencies in sample counts across confusion matrices suggest that certain models handled the evaluation set differently, complicating direct numerical comparisons. These differences may arise from variations in how evaluation frameworks process borderline predictions, apply probability thresholds, or manage batch-level outputs during inference. Therefore, confusion matrix–based insights were interpreted alongside ROC and class-specific metrics for a more reliable assessment. The WHFDL confusion Matrix confirmed its strong discriminative ability, with only 2 false positives and 3 false negatives (TN = 54, FP = 2, FN = 3, TP = 27), achieving both high sensitivity and specificity. CatB also produced strong results (TN = 84, FP = 8, FN = 10, TP = 39), though with a slightly higher false classification rate. RNN yielded similarly strong performance (TN = 82, FP = 10, FN = 8, TP = 41) but was ultimately more effective than LSTM, despite identical AUC scores of 0.9181. This distinction stems from RNN’s lower false negative count compared to LSTM (8 vs. 9), which is particularly critical in medical diagnostics where missing positive cases has severe implications. Conversely, Logistic Regression, although achieving perfect specificity (TN = 92, FP = 0), failed entirely in detecting GC cases (TP = 0, FN = 48), yielding the weakest confusion Matrix profile among all classifiers. Decision Tree similarly misclassified 17 GC samples (TP = 32, FN = 17), in Line with its low AUC of 0.75. CNN (AUC = 0.8622) also struggled to correctly identify cancer cases, resulting in 25 false negatives and 8 false positives.
These findings underscore the necessity of combining multiple evaluation strategies when assessing classifier performance in clinical contexts. While ROC and AUC offer valuable insight into overall discrimination, they do not reveal class-specific misclassification patterns or the practical clinical implications of false positives and negatives. Confusion matrices, though informative, are likewise insufficient in isolation. As emphasized throughout prior sections, class-level metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score provide crucial complementary information. Taken together, these evaluation tools confirm that WHFDL not only achieves the highest overall accuracy but also maintains the most balanced and reliable diagnostic performance across all metrics. Notably, rigorous verification of WHFDL’s classification matrix is essential. Standardization challenges in error reporting underscore the importance of transparent metric documentation. Subsequent studies should prioritize optimizing parameter configurations for weaker models and validating top-performing architectures across diverse patient cohorts to assess generalizability and translational viability.In the analysis exhibited in Fig.
10
, it is observed that the model’s accuracy decreases from approximately 94% to 76% under an FGSM (Fast Gradient Sign Method) adversarial attack with a perturbation magnitude (ε) of 0.05. This decline, representing a 10–20% drop in accuracy, is generally considered typical for models that have not undergone adversarial training. Within the academic and practical landscape of machine learning, such a decrease is viewed as an indicator of moderate vulnerability, signaling both a manageable challenge and an opportunity to further strengthen the model’s defenses. Lime and SHAP explanation
The SHAP method, rooted in cooperative game theory, offers a sophisticated and mathematically principled approach to interpreting machine learning models by quantifying the contribution of each feature to the model’s output. Through the computation of SHAP values, it assigns an additive importance score to every feature, capturing both the individual and interactive effects of features on the prediction. This property allows researchers to unravel complex, nonlinear dependencies among features, which is particularly valuable in high-dimensional models like deep neural networks. Its consistency, precision, and theoretical grounding make SHAP one of the most dependable tools for explaining black-box models.
In contrast, the LIME technique provides a flexible, model-agnostic interpretability framework that focuses on understanding model predictions locally around individual data points. By approximating the model’s behavior in the neighborhood of each observation using simple, interpretable surrogate models, such as linear regressions or decision trees, LIME enables the decomposition of the model’s output into understandable components. This local interpretability is particularly useful in high-stakes applications such as medical diagnostics and financial decision-making, where stakeholders require transparent and comprehensible explanations. LIME’s versatility across different model architectures and its intuitive presentation of feature importance have contributed to its widespread adoption in the field of explainable AI.

The calibration curves explanation
The calibration curve is a valuable analytical instrument for evaluating the probabilistic accuracy of Machine learning models, particularly in classification tasks. This curve is constructed by juxtaposing the predicted probabilities of the model against the observed frequencies of the corresponding events in the actual data. An ideally calibrated model would yield points that closely align with the diagonal reference Line, signifying that, for instance, a predicted probability of 0.7 indeed translates to approximately 70% of instances belonging to the positive class. This alignment ensures that the model’s outputs are both trustworthy and interpretable in terms of estimated probabilities. Employing a calibration curve enables researchers and data scientists to diagnose potential biases or miscalibrations within the model’s predictions. Furthermore, it provides a foundation for implementing post-hoc calibration methods, such as Platt Scaling or Isotonic Regression, to refine the model’s probabilistic outputs and enhance its real-world applicability, particularly in decision-making contexts where accurate risk assessment is essential.

This sparsity stems from the relatively small dataset and the use of a modest number of bins, factors that commonly lead to empty bins in probability ranges where predictions are sparse. Such a pattern is particularly prevalent in medical datasets, such as those concerning the diagnosis of gastric cancer, where predictions often cluster near the extremes, reflecting strong confidence in either the presence or absence of the disease. In this particular case, calibration points corresponding to higher probability predictions (e.g., between 0.7 and 0.8) are situated above the ideal diagonal line, indicating a tendency for the model to overestimate its confidence in high-probability scenarios. Although this optimism suggests that the model is somewhat overconfident in its predictions, the overall shape of the calibration curve still reflects a generally acceptable performance. Importantly, this type of miscalibration can often be mitigated through targeted recalibration strategies, thereby enhancing the model’s reliability in practical settings.

Adversarial vulnerability and integrated gradients explanation
Adversarial vulnerability is recognized as a critical challenge in machine learning, particularly in the context of deploying models in real-world applications. This phenomenon describes the susceptibility of models to seemingly insignificant, often imperceptible, perturbations in input data that can lead to substantial degradation in predictive accuracy. These so-called adversarial examples are usually generated through deliberate optimization processes that exploit the model’s decision boundaries, compelling it to produce erroneous outputs even though the altered inputs remain virtually indistinguishable from the originals to the human eye. This vulnerability is especially pronounced in complex architectures such as deep neural networks, highlighting a fundamental limitation in the generalizability and trustworthiness of these models. Consequently, understanding and addressing adversarial vulnerability is indispensable for enhancing the robustness and security of machine learning systems, ensuring they perform reliably under realistic conditions where malicious perturbations may be present.

Within the academic and practical landscape of machine learning, such a decrease is viewed as an indicator of moderate vulnerability, signaling both a manageable challenge and an opportunity to further strengthen the model’s defenses. While this drop reflects the model’s sensitivity to adversarial perturbations, it still aligns with expected performance levels. Clinical and biological explanations
In gastrointestinal cancer cells, researchers have frequently observed alterations in the levels of 1-Methyladenosine or its associated regulatory factors when compared to their normal counterparts, as detailed in [
95
]. Furthermore, a study employing metabolomics profiling has pinpointed changes in the levels of various acylcarnitine’s, notably long-chain forms like C18-Carnitine, in individuals diagnosed with gastric cancer, as reported in [
96
]. In addition, in another study [
97
], differences in carnitine and acylcarnitine derivatives including C18-Carnitine were observed in the blood of gastric cancer patients compared with healthy individuals. Also, the C18-Carnitine metabolic system is known to play a pivotal role in the metabolic plasticity of cancer cells in general, leading to the metabolic flexibility of cancer cells and making them more aggressive and able to metastasize [
98
].
Guanidine acetic acid (GAA) serves as the direct precursor for creatine, a compound vital for cellular energy management particularly within muscle and brain tissues, and its synthesis requires glycine and arginine [
99
]. A metabolomics investigation [
100
] indicated significant changes in creatine riboside in the more advanced stages of gastric cancer. Considering GAA's role as a creatine precursor, it is plausible that it indirectly contributes to this observation. It has been observed in multiple studies that Guanidinoacetate N-Methyltransferase (GAMT), the enzyme responsible for the conversion of guanidinoacetate to creatine, is downregulated in gastric cancer cells compared with normal gastric cells, which could lead to altered levels of guanidinoacetate and creatine deficiency [
101
,
102
]. The mechanisms involved in the variations in GAA serum levels and the role of GAA and creatine in gastric cancer could be studied in future works to address the observed controversy.
Hypoxanthine, a purine base, plays a role in both purine metabolism and nucleotide synthesis. It functions as an intermediary compound during the breakdown of ATP and GTP [
103
]. Research documented at [
104
] revealed variable concentrations of Hypoxanthine in the blood serum of individuals with gastric cancer, suggesting its potential utility as a diagnostic biomarker. NMN acts as a precursor to Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD +), a critical coenzyme involved in fundamental cellular processes such as metabolism and DNA repair [
105
]. In cancerous states, NAD + levels often become imbalanced, with cancer cells typically exhibiting increased amounts [
106
]. NAD + is essential for the survival and growth of cancer cells [
107
]. A study detailed at [
105
] showed altered expression patterns of genes related to NAD + metabolism (NMRGs) within gastric cancer tissues and cell lines. Interestingly, when these cell lines (AGS and MKN45) were treated with β-nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), their proliferation rates increased.
Succinate is an intermediate within the mitochondrial tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, a key process in energy generation [
108
]. It can also behave as an oncometabolite, altering the activities of signaling pathways such as the MAPK/ERK pathway in the tumor microenvironment (TME), thereby promoting angiogenesis and metastasis in cancers such as gastric cancer [
109
,
110
]. A review [
111
] addressed succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) deficiency in wild-type gastrointestinal stromal tumors, which leads to changes in succinate levels. It is also noted that SDH deficiency can occur in gastric cancer cells [
112
].

Lime and SHAP explanation
The SHAP method, rooted in cooperative game theory, offers a sophisticated and mathematically principled approach to interpreting machine learning models by quantifying the contribution of each feature to the model’s output. Through the computation of SHAP values, it assigns an additive importance score to every feature, capturing both the individual and interactive effects of features on the prediction. This property allows researchers to unravel complex, nonlinear dependencies among features, which is particularly valuable in high-dimensional models like deep neural networks. Its consistency, precision, and theoretical grounding make SHAP one of the most dependable tools for explaining black-box models.
In contrast, the LIME technique provides a flexible, model-agnostic interpretability framework that focuses on understanding model predictions locally around individual data points. By approximating the model’s behavior in the neighborhood of each observation using simple, interpretable surrogate models, such as linear regressions or decision trees, LIME enables the decomposition of the model’s output into understandable components. This local interpretability is particularly useful in high-stakes applications such as medical diagnostics and financial decision-making, where stakeholders require transparent and comprehensible explanations. LIME’s versatility across different model architectures and its intuitive presentation of feature importance have contributed to its widespread adoption in the field of explainable AI.

The calibration curves explanation
The calibration curve is a valuable analytical instrument for evaluating the probabilistic accuracy of Machine learning models, particularly in classification tasks. This curve is constructed by juxtaposing the predicted probabilities of the model against the observed frequencies of the corresponding events in the actual data. An ideally calibrated model would yield points that closely align with the diagonal reference Line, signifying that, for instance, a predicted probability of 0.7 indeed translates to approximately 70% of instances belonging to the positive class. This alignment ensures that the model’s outputs are both trustworthy and interpretable in terms of estimated probabilities. Employing a calibration curve enables researchers and data scientists to diagnose potential biases or miscalibrations within the model’s predictions. Furthermore, it provides a foundation for implementing post-hoc calibration methods, such as Platt Scaling or Isotonic Regression, to refine the model’s probabilistic outputs and enhance its real-world applicability, particularly in decision-making contexts where accurate risk assessment is essential.

This sparsity stems from the relatively small dataset and the use of a modest number of bins, factors that commonly lead to empty bins in probability ranges where predictions are sparse. Such a pattern is particularly prevalent in medical datasets, such as those concerning the diagnosis of gastric cancer, where predictions often cluster near the extremes, reflecting strong confidence in either the presence or absence of the disease. In this particular case, calibration points corresponding to higher probability predictions (e.g., between 0.7 and 0.8) are situated above the ideal diagonal line, indicating a tendency for the model to overestimate its confidence in high-probability scenarios. Although this optimism suggests that the model is somewhat overconfident in its predictions, the overall shape of the calibration curve still reflects a generally acceptable performance. This phenomenon describes the susceptibility of models to seemingly insignificant, often imperceptible, perturbations in input data that can lead to substantial degradation in predictive accuracy. These so-called adversarial examples are usually generated through deliberate optimization processes that exploit the model’s decision boundaries, compelling it to produce erroneous outputs even though the altered inputs remain virtually indistinguishable from the originals to the human eye. This vulnerability is especially pronounced in complex architectures such as deep neural networks, highlighting a fundamental limitation in the generalizability and trustworthiness of these models. Consequently, understanding and addressing adversarial vulnerability is indispensable for enhancing the robustness and security of machine learning systems, ensuring they perform reliably under realistic conditions where malicious perturbations may be present.

Clinical and biological explanations
In gastrointestinal cancer cells, researchers have frequently observed alterations in the levels of 1-Methyladenosine or its associated regulatory factors when compared to their normal counterparts, as detailed in [
95
]. Furthermore, a study employing metabolomics profiling has pinpointed changes in the levels of various acylcarnitine’s, notably long-chain forms like C18-Carnitine, in individuals diagnosed with gastric cancer, as reported in [
96
]. In addition, in another study [
97
], differences in carnitine and acylcarnitine derivatives including C18-Carnitine were observed in the blood of gastric cancer patients compared with healthy individuals. Also, the C18-Carnitine metabolic system is known to play a pivotal role in the metabolic plasticity of cancer cells in general, leading to the metabolic flexibility of cancer cells and making them more aggressive and able to metastasize [
98
].
Guanidine acetic acid (GAA) serves as the direct precursor for creatine, a compound vital for cellular energy management particularly within muscle and brain tissues, and its synthesis requires glycine and arginine [
99
]. A metabolomics investigation [
100
] indicated significant changes in creatine riboside in the more advanced stages of gastric cancer. Considering GAA's role as a creatine precursor, it is plausible that it indirectly contributes to this observation. It has been observed in multiple studies that Guanidinoacetate N-Methyltransferase (GAMT), the enzyme responsible for the conversion of guanidinoacetate to creatine, is downregulated in gastric cancer cells compared with normal gastric cells, which could lead to altered levels of guanidinoacetate and creatine deficiency [
101
,
102
]. The mechanisms involved in the variations in GAA serum levels and the role of GAA and creatine in gastric cancer could be studied in future works to address the observed controversy.
Hypoxanthine, a purine base, plays a role in both purine metabolism and nucleotide synthesis. It functions as an intermediary compound during the breakdown of ATP and GTP [
103
]. Research documented at [
104
] revealed variable concentrations of Hypoxanthine in the blood serum of individuals with gastric cancer, suggesting its potential utility as a diagnostic biomarker. NMN acts as a precursor to Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD +), a critical coenzyme involved in fundamental cellular processes such as metabolism and DNA repair [
105
]. In cancerous states, NAD + levels often become imbalanced, with cancer cells typically exhibiting increased amounts [
106
]. NAD + is essential for the survival and growth of cancer cells [
107
]. A study detailed at [
105
] showed altered expression patterns of genes related to NAD + metabolism (NMRGs) within gastric cancer tissues and cell lines. Interestingly, when these cell lines (AGS and MKN45) were treated with β-nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), their proliferation rates increased.
Succinate is an intermediate within the mitochondrial tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, a key process in energy generation [
108
]. It can also behave as an oncometabolite, altering the activities of signaling pathways such as the MAPK/ERK pathway in the tumor microenvironment (TME), thereby promoting angiogenesis and metastasis in cancers such as gastric cancer [
109
,
110
]. A review [
111
] addressed succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) deficiency in wild-type gastrointestinal stromal tumors, which leads to changes in succinate levels. It is also noted that SDH deficiency can occur in gastric cancer cells [
112
].

Slight inconsistencies in sample counts across confusion matrices suggest that certain models handled the evaluation set differently, complicating direct numerical comparisons. These differences may arise from variations in how evaluation frameworks process borderline predictions, apply probability thresholds, or manage batch-level outputs during inference. Therefore, confusion matrix–based insights were interpreted alongside ROC and class-specific metrics for a more reliable assessment. The WHFDL confusion Matrix confirmed its strong discriminative ability, with only 2 false positives and 3 false negatives (TN = 54, FP = 2, FN = 3, TP = 27), achieving both high sensitivity and specificity. CatB also produced strong results (TN = 84, FP = 8, FN = 10, TP = 39), though with a slightly higher false classification rate. RNN yielded similarly strong performance (TN = 82, FP = 10, FN = 8, TP = 41) but was ultimately more effective than LSTM, despite identical AUC scores of 0.9181. This distinction stems from RNN’s lower false negative count compared to LSTM (8 vs. 9), which is particularly critical in medical diagnostics where missing positive cases has severe implications. Conversely, Logistic Regression, although achieving perfect specificity (TN = 92, FP = 0), failed entirely in detecting GC cases (TP = 0, FN = 48), yielding the weakest confusion Matrix profile among all classifiers. Decision Tree similarly misclassified 17 GC samples (TP = 32, FN = 17), in Line with its low AUC of 0.75. CNN (AUC = 0.8622) also struggled to correctly identify cancer cases, resulting in 25 false negatives and 8 false positives.
These findings underscore the necessity of combining multiple evaluation strategies when assessing classifier performance in clinical contexts. While ROC and AUC offer valuable insight into overall discrimination, they do not reveal class-specific misclassification patterns or the practical clinical implications of false positives and negatives. Confusion matrices, though informative, are likewise insufficient in isolation. As emphasized throughout prior sections, class-level metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score provide crucial complementary information. Taken together, these evaluation tools confirm that WHFDL not only achieves the highest overall accuracy but also maintains the most balanced and reliable diagnostic performance across all metrics. Notably, rigorous verification of WHFDL’s classification matrix is essential. Standardization challenges in error reporting underscore the importance of transparent metric documentation.
